positions/cappadocian-trinitarianism/nam: Cappadocian formulation: one ousia, three hypostases
positions/cappadocian-trinitarianism/one: God is one in essence (ousia) and three in hypostases, each person distinguished only by an incommunicable property: the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, the Spirit proceeding.
positions/cappadocian-trinitarianism/cor: Ousia (essence) names what is common; hypostasis names what is particular — as the general to the particular.
The Father is the ‘cause’ and source (monarchia) of Son and Spirit, but they are co-eternal and equal.
All divine actions toward the world are one action, from the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit — so there are not three gods.
The divine essence is incomprehensible; we know God through his energies and works, never by grasping his essence (against Eunomius).
The Spirit is homotimos (of equal honour) with Father and Son.
positions/cappadocian-trinitarianism/ori: Worked out c. 360–390 by Basil of Caesarea, his brother Gregory of Nyssa, their friend Gregory of Nazianzus, with their sister Macrina an influence on Nyssa; drawing on Athanasius and the Homoiousians, against the Anomoean Eunomius and the Pneumatomachians.
positions/cappadocian-trinitarianism/str: It resolved the terminological confusion of the 4th century, reconciling Nicenes and Homoiousians.
It safeguards both the Father's monarchy (one source) and the full equality of the persons.
Its apophatic emphasis (God's essence is unknowable) fits biblical reticence and answers Eunomius' rationalism.
The unity of divine action (Gregory of Nyssa, To Ablabius) explains why three persons are not three gods.
The ‘general/particular’ analogy (as humanity to Peter, James and John) seems to make the persons three instances of a genus — tritheism (as John Philoponus later concluded).
Western critics (and later Filioque defenders) argue that grounding unity in the Father's monarchy risks subordinating the Son and Spirit.
Some modern scholars argue the Cappadocians were less ‘social’ than 20th-century readers claim, so appeals to them are anachronistic.
positions/cappadocian-trinitarianism/res: Gregory of Nyssa explicitly denies that the analogy implies three gods, since divine nature is not divided or numbered like human nature and the persons' action is one.
The Father's monarchy is a monarchy of origin, not of rank; the Son and Spirit possess all that the Father has except being unbegotten.
positions/cappadocian-trinitarianism/con: Became the classical formulation of Eastern Orthodox Trinitarian theology and was received by the Council of Constantinople (381).
Its terms entered Latin as una essentia, tres personae (with lasting translation difficulties between hypostasis and persona).
Its distinction between essence and energies was developed by Gregory Palamas (14th c.).
positions/filioque/oneLine: The Holy Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father and the Son as from one principle — so the creed may say ‘who proceeds from the Father and the Son’.
positions/filioque/coreClaims/0: The Spirit is the Spirit of the Son as well as of the Father (Galatians 4:6; Romans 8:9); the Son sends and breathes the Spirit (John 15:26; 20:22).
positions/filioque/coreClaims/1: Divine persons are distinguished by relations of origin; unless the Spirit proceeds from the Son, Son and Spirit would not be distinguished from each other (Anselm, Aquinas).
positions/filioque/coreClaims/2: The Father is principally the source; the Son receives from the Father the capacity to breathe the Spirit (Augustine: principaliter from the Father).
positions/filioque/coreClaims/3: The Spirit is the mutual love and gift of Father and Son.
positions/filioque/origin: Taught by Latin fathers (Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine); inserted into the creed in Spain at Toledo III (589) against Arian subordination of the Son; spread in Frankish lands under Charlemagne; adopted in Rome's liturgy c. 1014; defined at Lyon II (1274) and Florence (1439).
positions/filioque/strongestArguments/0: It expresses the full equality of Father and Son: all that the Father has belongs to the Son (John 16:15), except being Father.
positions/filioque/strongestArguments/1: Scripture calls the Spirit ‘the Spirit of his Son’ and depicts the Son sending the Spirit.
positions/filioque/strongestArguments/2: Some Greek Fathers (Cyril of Alexandria, Maximus the Confessor) spoke of the Spirit proceeding ‘through the Son’, which Latins see as compatible.
positions/filioque/strongestArguments/3: Historically it guarded against Arianism in Visigothic Spain.
positions/filioque/strongestObjections/0: The original creed of 381 said ‘from the Father’; a single regional church may not alter an ecumenical creed (Council of Ephesus canon 7 forbids a different creed).
positions/filioque/strongestObjections/1: Two sources of the Spirit compromise the Father's monarchy, or else merge Father and Son into one impersonal principle (Photius).
positions/filioque/strongestObjections/2: It subordinates the Spirit to the Son, encouraging ‘Christomonism’ and an institutional, Spirit-neglecting ecclesiology (modern Orthodox critics such as Vladimir Lossky).
positions/filioque/strongestObjections/3: Pope Leo III himself (c. 810) had the original creed engraved on silver shields in St Peter's, refusing the insertion.
positions/filioque/responses/0: Latins argue the addition clarifies rather than changes the faith, and was made for pastoral need against Arians.
positions/filioque/responses/1: The 1995 Vatican clarification states that the Father is the sole ‘source without source’ and that the Latin procedit (from the Father and the Son) is not the same as the Greek ekporeuesthai (from the Father alone as origin).
positions/filioque/responses/2: Rome itself uses the creed without the Filioque in Greek and with Eastern Catholics; several Anglican provinces have proposed or adopted its omission.
positions/filioque/consequences/0: A major doctrinal grievance behind the East–West estrangement and the 1054 schism.
positions/filioque/consequences/1: Central agenda item at the reunion councils of Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439).
positions/filioque/consequences/2: Ongoing ecumenical dialogue: the 2003 North American Orthodox–Catholic statement concluded it need no longer be church-dividing if handled well.
positions/monopatrism/name: Monopatrism: procession from the Father alone (Eastern)
positions/monopatrism/oneLine: The Father alone is the eternal source and cause of the Son (by begetting) and of the Spirit (by procession); the Son's role in the Spirit's sending belongs to the economy or, at most, to an eternal manifestation ‘through the Son’.
positions/monopatrism/coreClaims/0: Each hypostatic property belongs to one person only: being unbegotten and causing belongs to the Father alone.
positions/monopatrism/coreClaims/1: John 15:26 says the Spirit ‘proceeds from the Father’; the Son ‘sends’ the Spirit in time (the economy).
positions/monopatrism/coreClaims/2: The Creed of 381, confirmed by later ecumenical councils, may not be changed except by an ecumenical council.
positions/monopatrism/coreClaims/3: The Spirit eternally shines forth or rests on the Son (Gregory of Cyprus, 13th c.), but takes origin from the Father alone.
positions/monopatrism/origin: Implicit in the Cappadocians' monarchy of the Father; formulated against the Latin Filioque by Patriarch Photius of Constantinople in his encyclical (867) and Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit; refined by Gregory of Cyprus and Gregory Palamas.
positions/monopatrism/strongestArguments: It keeps the exact words of Christ in John 15:26 and of the ecumenical creed.
It preserves the Father's monarchy, the Cappadocian guarantee of divine unity.
John of Damascus already wrote that the Spirit is ‘from the Father’ and ‘of the Son’, but ‘we do not say from the Son’ (Exact Exposition 1.8).
Ecclesially it guards conciliarity against a single see altering the common faith.
positions/monopatrism/strongestObjection: Latin theologians argue that without a relation of origin between Son and Spirit their distinction is undefined.
Scripture's ‘Spirit of the Son’ language suggests an eternal, not merely temporal, relation.
Some Greek Fathers (Cyril, Maximus) used ‘through the Son’ language that seems to give the Son an eternal role.
positions/monopatrism/responses/0: Orthodox theologians answer that persons are distinguished by their unique mode of origin from the Father (begetting vs procession), which suffices.
positions/monopatrism/responses/1: Gregory of Cyprus and Palamas distinguish eternal procession (from the Father alone) from an eternal manifestation or radiance through the Son — accepting ‘through the Son’ in that sense.
positions/monopatrism/responses/2: Maximus the Confessor's Letter to Marinus defended the Western usage only as meaning the Son is not the cause.
positions/monopatrism/consequences/0: Defines the Orthodox side of a millennium-long dispute, rehearsed at Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439).
positions/monopatrism/consequences/1: Shapes Orthodox pneumatology and ecclesiology (emphasis on the Spirit's freedom and the conciliar church).
positions/monopatrism/consequences/2: Agreed statements since the 1990s have narrowed but not closed the gap.
positions/classical-trinitarianism/oneLi: One utterly simple God subsists as three persons who are nothing other than subsisting relations of origin — paternity, filiation and spiration — known to us only through revelation.
positions/classical-trinitarianism/coreC: The divine essence is one and numerically identical in all three persons; the persons are not parts or instances of a kind.
The persons are distinguished only by opposed relations of origin (Father–Son; Father and Son–Spirit).
All works of the Trinity toward creation are undivided (opera ad extra indivisa sunt), though appropriated to particular persons.
Analogies (memory–understanding–will; lover–beloved–love) are aids to contemplation, not proofs.
The Trinity is a revealed mystery beyond natural reason.
positions/classical-trinitarianism/origi: Rooted in Augustine's De Trinitate (c. 400–420) and the Athanasian Creed (Quicunque vult, c. 500), systematised by Anselm, Peter Lombard and Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I, qq. 27–43), confirmed at Lateran IV (1215) against Joachim of Fiore, and received by Reformation confessions.
positions/classical-trinitarianism/propo: contemporary: Gilles Emery, Matthew Levering, Fred Sanders (broadly)
positions/classical-trinitarianism/stron: It guards divine unity rigorously, avoiding any hint of three gods.
It offers a coherent account of how persons are distinguished (relations) without dividing the essence.
It has shaped Western liturgy, mysticism and theology for 1,500 years and has deep patristic roots in both East and West.
Its doctrine of inseparable operations explains biblical texts in which Father, Son and Spirit all create, raise and indwell.
Eastern critics argue that it begins with the one essence and struggles to reach real persons, tending toward modalism.
Social Trinitarians say ‘subsisting relations’ are too abstract to be persons who love and speak to one another, as the Gospels depict.
Rahner complained that it made the Trinity irrelevant to piety: most Christians would be ‘mere monotheists’ in practice.
Analytic philosophers question whether ‘simple’ and ‘three really distinct persons’ are logically consistent.
positions/classical-trinitarianism/respo: Defenders argue the ‘Western starts with essence, East with persons’ contrast (de Régnon paradigm) is a 19th-century oversimplification.
Augustine and Aquinas insist the persons are really distinct and mutually indwelling; relations are not less but more personal than ‘individuals’.
Classical theologians answer that modern ‘persons’ (centres of consciousness) is a different concept from patristic hypostasis, and importing it produces tritheism.
positions/classical-trinitarianism/conse: Foundation of Western dogmatic theology, catechisms and the Athanasian Creed's place in Western liturgy.
Supported the theological rationale for the Filioque.
A reference point in contemporary debates with social Trinitarians and analytic philosophers.
